Eves Extension

GeometryCirclesInvariants
Game: A red dot travels around a shape whose sides all touch one circle; watch where it ends up.
How to play: Drag the blue dots on the circle or the red start dot, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Change the number of sides with N.
Look for the math

A dot goes for a walk around a polygon whose sides all touch one circle. Sometimes the second trip lands on exactly the same spots; sometimes it does not. The number of sides decides which.

Sides that touch a circle

The blue dots are points of tangency: each side of the polygon just grazes the circle there. The yellow dots are the corners where neighbouring sides meet. To move the red dot from one side to the next, the applet turns it about a corner through that corner's angle — a rotation that keeps its distance from the corner.

Equal tangents from a corner

From one corner, the two lines touching the incircle have equal lengths. If the two tangents from corner i have length t(i), the side between corners i and i+1 is t(i) + t(i+1). Adding every other side gives the same total as adding the ones in between:

a1 + a3 + a5 + ... = a2 + a4 + a6 + ...

For four sides this is the familiar rule that opposite sides add up to the same amount. The logic test checked it for every even number of sides from 4 to 20, on many irregular shapes.

Even or odd?

After one lap the rotations add up to a whole turn when the number of sides is even, so the whole trip acts like a slide. The slide is zero exactly when the alternating sum above is zero — which it always is here, whatever the start. With an odd number of sides the rotations add up to a half turn, which has just one fixed point. For a polygon with an incircle that point is a point of tangency; starting anywhere else leaves a gap. The test confirmed both statements for every N from 3 to 19. One tiny quirk: the bytecode computes one last rotation of the first corner and throws the result away, so this port leaves it out too; nothing is drawn from it.

An incircle is not required

For a quadrilateral, equal opposite sums are enough to guarantee an incircle. For six or more sides they are only necessary. The test builds a hexagon whose alternating sum is zero but whose sides cannot all touch one circle, and its two loops still match; it also finds a pentagon with no incircle whose loops close at the right start. A triangle is rigid, but a longer polygon can be bent into the same side lengths without any incircle — exactly the point of the original note.

Try N = 6 and drag the red dot far away: the second loop still matches. Then switch to N = 5 and press Start on a tangency point.
